query: Consider the following context: Constituent phases and their corresponding phase transformations are important in developing alloys. In that context, which method can be used for control of phase evolution in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni HEAs, and why?

generation.hypothesis: We hypothesize that adjusting heat treatment parameters (time, temperature, cooling rates) in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys will systematically alter the fractions and morphologies of BCC/B2 phases, thereby controlling phase evolution and enabling customization of mechanical properties.
generation.material_initial_state: Arc- or induction-melted Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloy in as-cast condition.
generation.intervention: Vary solution treatment temperature from 800 °C to 1000 °C followed by controlled cooling protocols (e.g., water quenching vs. furnace cooling).
generation.conditions: Annealing under an inert or vacuum atmosphere for durations ranging from 1 hour to multiple hours, systematically varying cooling rates from rapid quench to slow cool.
generation.structural_mediator: Nucleation and growth of BCC/B2 phases in the Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni matrix during thermal exposure.
generation.mechanism: Thermally activated diffusion reshuffles the distribution and bonding of key elements, prompting phase transformations that modify microstructure and thus mechanical properties.
generation.predicted_outcome: A tailored microstructure with tunable fractions of BCC and ordered B2 constituents, achieving improved control over mechanical properties such as hardness and yield strength.
generation.baseline: In the as-cast state, the alloy may exhibit multiple phases and less optimized mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: Transformation kinetics slow below ~800 °C, and at very high temperatures (>1200 °C), excessive coarsening or unexpected phase formation can occur without careful control of cooling rates.
generation.uncertainty: Local chemical inhomogeneities and sluggish diffusion effects may alter transformation pathways, and the precise phase fraction evolution cannot be fully predicted without further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy samples with identical initial compositions. Subject each set to distinct heat treatment schedules at the specified temperature ranges and cooling protocols. Characterize microstructures using XRD, SEM, and TEM to observe differences in BCC/B2 phases and measure changes in hardness and yield strength by standard mechanical testing.
measurements: Yield strength via uniaxial compression tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the measured phase fractions and properties do not vary in correlation with the heat treatment parameters, the hypothesis that controlling time-temperature-cooling modifies phase evolution is refuted.

cited_evidence.text:
High-entropy alloys (HEAs) have attracted a lot of attention in recent years, due to the unique combinations of structural, physical and chemical properties of these alloys [1] – [3] . HEAs usually form simple structures such as body-centered cubic (BCC) (e.g. TaNbHfZrTi [4] , NbTaVWZr [5] etc.) or face-centered cubic (FCC) (e.g., CoCrCuFeNi [6] , CoCrFeMnNi [7] etc.) solid solutions. The large number of the alloying elements in near-equiatomic proportions result in high configurational entropy in these solid solutions. However, these alloys can decompose to multiple phases upon changing the composition or annealing at different temperatures or a combination of both [8] – [10] . Such a phase decomposition is often the result of the complex interplay of configurational entropy of mixing with the enthalpies of mixing of the constituent elements. Additionally, such multiphase microstructures are more likely to exhibit the desired properties for real engineering applications. Hence, tuning the composition and fractions of phases is critical for achieving the desired properties [10] , [11] .
